claim: When mice run, activity in their primary visual cortex (V1) is strongly modulated.
source: When mice run, activity in their primary visual cortex (V1) is strongly modulated.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript and by data presented in the figures.

claim: Running-correlated modulations of marmoset V1 were small and tended to be slightly suppressive.
source: In contrast to mouse, running-correlated modulations of marmoset V1 were small and tended to be slightly suppressive.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Population-level gain modulations were strongly correlated with running in mice.
source: Population-level analyses revealed trial-to-trial fluctuations of shared gain across V1 in both species, but while strongly correlated with running in mice, gain modulations were smaller and more often negatively correlated with running in marmosets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the shared gain model analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Gain modulations in marmosets were smaller and more often negatively correlated with running.
source: Population-level analyses revealed trial-to-trial fluctuations of shared gain across V1 in both species, but while strongly correlated with running in mice, gain modulations were smaller and more often negatively correlated with running in marmosets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the shared gain model analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Activity in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) depends as much on whether the mouse is running or stationary as on what visual stimulus is shown.
source: Recent work in mice, a major mammalian model system in neuroscience, has called for a re-evaluation of this distinction, given recent demonstrations that activity in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) depends as much on whether the mouse is running or stationary as on what visual stimulus is shown (Niell and Stryker, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Niell and Stryker, 2010.

claim: Neurons in V1 of virtually all mammals are selective for simple image features.
source: Neurons in V1 of virtually all mammals are selective for simple image features, a presumably critical early step of image processing that continues throughout a hierarchy of visual brain areas (Rosa and Krubitzer, 1999; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991), and this is true of mice as well (Niell and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rosa and Krubitzer, 1999; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; and Niell and Stryker, 2008.

claim: Primates are more fundamentally visual organisms than rodents, with exquisite acuity and specialized functional characteristics such as foveas.
source: Although rodents certainly rely on vision for important behaviors (Hoy et al., 2016; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), primates are more fundamentally visual organisms, with exquisite acuity and specialized functional characteristics such as foveas and corresponding high-resolution representations of the central visual field in V1 (Land and Fernald, 1992), in addition to a larger network of areas involved in vision (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoy et al., 2016; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013; Land and Fernald, 1992; and Felleman and Van Essen, 1991.

claim: Marmosets were head-fixed, placed on a wheel-based treadmill suited to their arboreal nature.
source: Marmosets were head-fixed, placed on a wheel-based treadmill suited to their arboreal nature (Figure 1a), and alternated between running and not running while we presented various visual stimuli designed to assess the properties and responsiveness of V1 neurons (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, supported by Figure 1a showing the apparatus.

claim: Receptive fields were mapped in marmoset V1 within the central few degrees of vision, with sizes expected at those eccentricities (1–5°).
source: In V1 of both marmosets, we found receptive fields within the central few degrees of vision, with sizes expected at those eccentricities (1–5°, Figure 1f, blue and green; these can be compared to those in mouse, Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the receptive field mapping data shown in Figure 1c and 1f.

claim: Marmoset V1 neurons responded robustly to oriented gratings and exhibited orientation- (and sometimes direction-) selectivity.
source: As expected for primary visual cortex, marmoset V1 (both well-isolated single units and well-tuned multi-unit clusters) responded robustly to oriented gratings and exhibited orientation- (and sometimes direction-) selectivity (Yu and Rosa, 2014; Sengpiel et al., 1996), similar to that in the mouse V1 dataset (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by the orientation tuning data shown in Figure 1h and citations to Yu and Rosa, 2014; Sengpiel et al., 1996.

claim: In marmosets, the distribution of correlations between V1 activity and running was subtly but reliably negative (median = −0.033, p=0.034, n=27).
source: For marmosets, the distribution of correlations between V1 activity and running was subtly but reliably negative (Figure 2f, median = −0.033, p=0.034, stat = 101, n = 27, Mann–Whitney U test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: In mouse V1, the geometric mean ratio of firing rate during running versus stationary for responses to preferred stimuli was 1.523 (95% CI [1.469, 1.579], n=743 tuned units).
source: This analysis confirmed, in mouse, a tendency for large response increases during running to both the preferred orientation stimulus (Figure 3a, geometric mean ratio [running/stationary] = 1.523, 95% CI [1.469, 1.579], n = 743 tuned units)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In mouse V1, 69% of units (803/1168) showed increased firing rate during running and 10% (115/1168) showed decreased firing rate.
source: Many individual units had significant running modulations and were more often increases rather than decreases (803/1168 [69%] increased firing rate and 115/1168 [10%] decreased, bootstrapped t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of individual units in mouse V1.

claim: In marmoset V1, there was a modest decrease in response to the preferred stimulus during running (geometric mean ratio = 0.899, 95% CI [0.851, 0.949], n=228 tuned units).
source: In marmoset V1, there was again a modest decrease evident in the response to the preferred stimulus (Figure 3c; geometric mean ratio [running/stationary] = 0.899, 95% CI [0.851, 0.949], n = 228 tuned units).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of the data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In marmoset V1, 22% of units (172/786) showed increased firing rate during running and 20% (161/786) showed decreased firing rate.
source: The number of significantly modulated units was relatively small and was more balanced between decreases and increases in firing rate (172/786 [22%] increased and 161/786 [20%] decreased, bootstrapped t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of individual units in marmoset V1.

claim: In mice, shared gain was higher during running than stationary (mean difference 0.970 [0.761, 1.225], p~0).
source: Furthermore, in the mouse, shared gain was higher for running than stationary as estimated during stimulus presentations (mean difference 0.970 [0.761, 1.225], p~0, stat 8.017, t-test), demonstrating that a substantial portion of modulations of mouse V1 can be explained by a shared gain term that increases with running (Figure 4f, orange point).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of the shared gain model shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In marmosets, shared gain was slightly but reliably lower when running (mean difference = −0.125 [−0.203, −0.059], p=0.002).
source: In marmoset, shared gain was slightly but reliably lower when running (mean difference = −0.125 [-0.203, -0.059], p=0.002, stat = −3.360, t-test, Figure 4f, blue point)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of the shared gain model shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Population-level gain modulations are likely a general principle of mammalian V1 function.
source: This was true in both species, bolstering the emerging notion that population-level gain modulations are a general principle of mammalian V1 function (Whiteway et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2015; Arandia-Romero et al., 2016; Goris et al., 2014; Ferguson and Cardin, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the shared gain model results in both species and citations to previous work.

claim: Peripheral marmoset V1 neurons had slightly higher stimulus-driven responses during running (geometric mean ratio = 1.129 [1.068, 1.194], n=147).
source: Analyzing neurons with peripheral receptive fields separately revealed a difference in running modulations between these retinotopically distinct portions of V1: peripheral neurons had slightly higher stimulus-driven responses during running (aggregating over all stimuli, geometric mean ratio [running/stationary] = 1.129 [1.068, 1.194], n = 147; difference with the central units was significant, p=2.100e-03, stat = 12376, Mann–Whitney U test)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of peripheral V1 neurons in marmoset.

claim: The difference in running modulation between peripheral and central marmoset V1 units was significant (p=2.100e-03).
source: peripheral neurons had slightly higher stimulus-driven responses during running (aggregating over all stimuli, geometric mean ratio [running/stationary] = 1.129 [1.068, 1.194], n = 147; difference with the central units was significant, p=2.100e-03, stat = 12376, Mann–Whitney U test)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between peripheral and central V1 neurons in marmoset.

claim: Saccades were slightly more frequent during running in marmosets (2.653 Hz [2.600, 2.697]) compared to stationary (2.525 Hz [2.475, 2.573]).
source: In short, saccades were slightly more frequent and larger during running (saccade frequency during running: 2.653 Hz, 95% CI [2.600, 2.697]; stationary/not running: 2.525 Hz [2.475, 2.573]; saccade magnitude during running: 9.261° [9.140, 9.374]; stationary/not running: 8.337° [8.190, 8.470]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of eye movements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Saccade magnitude was larger during running in marmosets (9.261° [9.140, 9.374]) compared to stationary (8.337° [8.190, 8.470]).
source: In short, saccades were slightly more frequent and larger during running (saccade frequency during running: 2.653 Hz, 95% CI [2.600, 2.697]; stationary/not running: 2.525 Hz [2.475, 2.573]; saccade magnitude during running: 9.261° [9.140, 9.374]; stationary/not running: 8.337° [8.190, 8.470]).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of eye movements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Differences in retinal stimulation due to differences in eye movements are unlikely to explain running-correlated suppression of V1 activity in marmosets.
source: Our initial analyses found that differences in retinal stimulation due to differences in eye movements are unlikely to explain running-correlated suppression of V1 activity.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of eye movements and their predicted effects on neural activity.

claim: The predicted spike rate increase during running based on saccades was 0.05 Hz (<1% gain), which cannot explain the observed decreases in V1 activity.
source: On the aggregate, saccades slightly increased activity (predicted spike rate increase during running based on saccades = 0.05 Hz; expressed as gain, <1%), and thus cannot explain the sign or magnitude of the subtle decreases we observed.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from regression analysis of saccade effects on neural activity.

claim: Pupil size was approximately 8% larger during running in marmosets.
source: Pupil size was ∼8% larger during running.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of pupil size shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The finding that pupil size is larger during running is consistent with the idea that marmosets were in a higher arousal state during running.
source: This finding is consistent with the idea that the marmosets were in a higher arousal state during running.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil size data based on established knowledge about pupil size and arousal.

claim: The primate-rodent difference in the magnitude and sign of V1 gain modulations is consistent with known differences in neuromodulatory inputs related to arousal in rodent and primate V1.
source: The primate-rodent difference in the magnitude and sign of V1 gain modulations we observed is in fact consistent with known differences in neuromodulatory inputs related to arousal in rodent and primate V1 (Disney and Robert, 2019; Coppola and Disney, 2018).
evidence: This claim connects the observed differences to mechanistic knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In primates, the locations of ACh receptors allow cholinergic inputs to increase the activity of the majority of GABAergic neurons and hence suppress net activity via inhibition.
source: In primates, the locations of ACh receptors allow cholinergic inputs to increase the activity of the majority of GABAergic neurons and hence suppress net activity via inhibition (Disney et al., 2007; Lien and Scanziani, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Disney et al., 2007 and Lien and Scanziani, 2013.

claim: Pharmacologically and anatomically distinct cholinergic influences in rodent likely exert more complex effects on net activity, including disinhibition which can increase net activity.
source: but pharmacologically and anatomically distinct cholinergic influences in rodent likely exert more complex effects on net activity, including disinhibition which can increase net activity (Pakan et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2014; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pakan et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2014; and Pfeffer et al., 2013.

claim: Running does not affect V1 activity in marmosets like it does in mouse.
source: In short, running does not affect V1 activity in marmosets like it does in mouse.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the data presented.

claim: The large, typically positive correlations between running and V1 activity often found in mice are simply not evident in marmosets.
source: The large, typically positive correlations between running and V1 activity often found in mice are simply not evident in marmosets.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the comparative data in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: In the foveal representation in marmoset V1, responses on average were slightly smaller during running.
source: In the foveal representation in V1 – where we made the majority of our recordings – responses on average were slightly smaller during running
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for foveal V1 based on the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In the peripheral representation of marmoset V1, responses were slightly larger during running.
source: in the peripheral representation, responses were slightly larger.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings for peripheral V1 based on the Neuropixels recordings.

claim: The same shared-gain model improved accounts of both mouse and marmoset V1 activity.
source: The same shared-gain model improved accounts of both mouse and marmoset V1 activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Population-level gain modulations likely reflect modulatory inputs associated with behavioral state and arousal.
source: These population-level gain modulations likely reflect modulatory inputs associated with behavioral state and arousal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the shared gain model results based on established knowledge.

claim: The primate foveal representation might be functionally unique, but the primate peripheral representation might be more functionally similar to that of mouse V1.
source: An intriguing conjecture is that the primate foveal representation might be functionally unique, but that the primate peripheral representation might be more functionally similar to that of mouse V1 (Horrocks et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differences between foveal and peripheral V1 in marmosets, with a citation to Horrocks et al., 2022.

claim: Experiments were performed on two common marmosets (one male, 'marmoset G', and one female, 'marmoset B', both aged 2 years).
source: We performed electrophysiological recordings in V1 of two common marmosets (one male, 'marmoset G', and one female, 'marmoset B', both aged 2 years).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Both marmoset subjects had chronically implanted N-form arrays inserted into left V1.
source: Both subjects had chronically implanted N-form arrays (Modular Bionics, Modular Bionics, Berkeley, CA) inserted into left V1.
evidence: This is a description of the recording method.

claim: Additional recordings were performed using Neuropixels 1.0 probes acutely inserted into small craniotomies.
source: Additional recordings were also performed using Neuropixels 1.0 probes (Jun et al., 2017) acutely inserted into small craniotomies (procedure described below).
evidence: This is a description of an additional recording method, with a citation to Jun et al., 2017.

claim: The monitor used in the experiments had a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz.
source: Subjects perched quadrupedally on a 12″ diameter wheel while head-fixed facing a 24″ LCD (BenQ) monitor (resolution = 1920 × 1080 pixels, refresh rate = 120 Hz) corrected to have a linear gamma function, at a distance of 36 cm (pixels per degree = 26.03) in a dark room.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Eye position was recorded via an Eyelink 1000 eye tracker sampling at 1 kHz.
source: Eye position was recorded via an Eyelink 1000 eye tracker (SR Research) sampling at 1 kHz.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracking method.

claim: Spike sorting on data acquired using N-Form arrays was performed using in-house code to track and merge data from identified single units across multiple recording sessions.
source: Spike sorting on data acquired using N-Form arrays was performed using in-house code to track and merge data from identified single units across multiple recording sessions (Muthmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, with a citation to Muthmann et al., 2021.

claim: Spike sorting for data acquired using Neuropixels probes was performed using Kilosort 2.5.
source: Spike sorting for data acquired using Neuropixels probes was performed using Kilosort 2.5.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Chronic N-Form arrays consisted of 16 shanks arrayed in a 4 × 4 grid with shanks evenly spaced 0.4 mm apart.
source: Chronic array recordings were performed using 64-channel chronically implanted 3D N-Form arrays consisting of 16 shanks arrayed in a 4 × 4 grid with shanks evenly spaced 0.4 mm apart (Modular Bionics, Berkeley).
evidence: This is a description of the recording electrode array.

claim: Well-isolated single units were detectable on the N-Form arrays in excess of 6 months after the initial implantation procedure.
source: Well-isolated single units were detectable on the arrays in excess of 6 months after the initial implantation procedure.
evidence: This is a statement about the longevity of the chronic recordings.

claim: Neuropixels 1.0 probes consist of 384 recording channels that can individually be configured to record signals from 960 selectable sites along a 10 mm long, 70 × 24 µm cross-sectional straight shank.
source: Acute Neuropixels recordings were performed using standard Neuropixels 1.0 electrodes (IMEC, Leuven, Belgium). Each probe consists of 384 recording channels that can individually be configured to record signals from 960 selectable sites along a 10 mm long, 70 × 24 µm cross-sectional straight shank.
evidence: This is a description of the Neuropixels probe specifications.

claim: Mouse data were downloaded from the publicly available Visual Coding database at https://portal.brain-map.org/explore/circuits/visual-coding-neuropixels.
source: Mouse data were downloaded from the publicly available Visual Coding database at https://portal.brain-map.org/explore/circuits/visual-coding-neuropixels.
evidence: This is a description of the source of the mouse data.

claim: The same analysis code was used to analyze mouse and marmoset data.
source: We used the same analysis code to analyze these data and the marmoset data we collected.
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis methodology to ensure comparability.

claim: Trials for all stimuli were 20 s long with a 500 ms inter-trial interval.
source: Trials for all stimuli were 20 s long with a 500 ms ITI and a 20-s-long natural image interleaved every fifth trial to keep the subject engaged.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Marmosets were rewarded at set locomotion distance intervals to elicit sufficiently reliable and frequent running behavior.
source: To elicit sufficiently reliable and frequent running behavior, subjects were rewarded at set locomotion distance intervals unrelated to the stimulus or gaze behavior (typical rewards were 50–70 µL and distance required to achieve a reward usually varied between 20 and 75 cm; reward amounts and intervals were adjusted daily to maximally motivate the subject).
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral training method.

claim: Marmosets naturally direct their gaze towards the faces of other marmosets when allowed to free-view with little-to-no training.
source: Marmosets naturally direct their gaze towards the faces of other marmosets when allowed to free-view with little-to-no training, allowing for the experimenter to adjust the calibration offset and gain manually between pattern presentations.
evidence: This is a statement about marmoset behavior used for eyetracking calibration.

claim: The primary stimulus consisted of full-field drifting gratings optimized to drive marmoset V1 with 3 separate spatial frequencies, 2 drift speeds, and 12 orientations.
source: The primary stimulus consisted of full-field drifting gratings. Gratings were optimized to drive marmoset V1 with 3 separate spatial frequencies (one, two, and four cycles per degree), 2 drift speeds (1 or 2° per second), and 12 orientations (evenly spaced 30° intervals).
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimuli used.

claim: A spatiotemporal receptive field mapping stimulus, consisting of sparse dot noise, was shown during each recording session.
source: A spatiotemporal receptive field mapping stimulus, consisting of sparse dot noise, was shown during each recording session. One hundred 1° white and black dots were presented at 50% contrast at random points on the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the receptive field mapping method.

claim: Marmosets freely viewed the sparse noise stimulus, and receptive fields were estimated using forward correlation correcting for eye position offline.
source: Marmosets freely viewed the stimulus, and we corrected for eye position offline to estimate the spatial receptive fields using forward correlation (Yates et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the receptive field estimation method, with a citation to Yates et al., 2021.

claim: Stimuli with considerably higher spatial frequencies were used for marmosets than for mice because the spatial frequency tunings of marmoset and mouse V1 neurons are starkly different.
source: Because the spatial frequency tunings of marmoset and mouse V1 neurons are starkly different, we used stimuli with considerably higher spatial frequencies than in the mouse experiments.
evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological difference based on known differences in visual systems.

claim: Marmoset V1 receptive fields are much smaller than in mouse.
source: Relatedly, marmoset V1 receptive fields are much smaller than in mouse.
evidence: This is a statement about a known difference between the species.

claim: Responses in marmoset V1 were likely affected by substantial amounts of surround suppression because full-field stimuli were used.
source: Because we used full-field stimuli (to match mouse experiments), responses in marmoset V1 were likely affected by substantial amounts of surround suppression, which would reduce overall responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of the stimulus choice on neural responses.

claim: A reward scheme was incorporated to motivate marmoset subjects to run more frequently.
source: We therefore incorporated a reward scheme to motivate the subjects to run more frequently.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological adaptation for marmosets.

claim: For the analyses in Figure 2, sessions were included if they contained more than 250 trials and a proportion of trials running was not less than 10% or greater than 90%.
source: For the analyses shown in Figure 2, sessions were included if they contained more than 250 trials and a proportion of trials running was not less than 10% or greater than 90%.
evidence: This is a description of the data inclusion criteria.

claim: For the mouse dataset, the inclusion criteria yielded 25/32 sessions.
source: For the mouse dataset, this yielded 25/32 sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result of applying the inclusion criteria.

claim: For the marmoset dataset, the inclusion criteria yielded 27/34 sessions.
source: For the marmoset dataset, this yielded 27/34 sessions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result of applying the inclusion criteria.

claim: For unit-wise analyses in Figure 3, super-sessioned units were included if they had more than 300 trials of data and a mean firing rate of >1 spike/s.
source: For the unit-wise analyses in Figure 3, super-sessioned units were included for analysis if they had more than 300 trials of data and a mean firing rate of >1 spike/s.
evidence: This is a description of the unit inclusion criteria.

claim: The unit inclusion criteria yielded 1168/2015 units in mouse and 786/1837 units in marmoset.
source: This yielded 1168/2015 units in mouse and 786/1837 units in marmoset.
evidence: This is a quantitative result of applying the unit inclusion criteria.

claim: To assess eye movement effects, the number of saccades and average saccade size were calculated for each stimulus presentation and regressed against spike count.
source: To assess whether and how eye movements might differ between running and stationary periods (and perhaps account for some or all of the running-correlated modulations of V1 response), we started by counting the number of saccades within a bin corresponding to each stimulus presentation (from 0.2 s before stimulus onset to 0.1 after offset), as well as calculating the average saccade size (vector magnitude) of those saccades. We then regressed these terms against the spike count in each bin, allowing us to estimate the effect of eye movements in units of spike rate (Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method for eye movement effects.

claim: Similar shared-gain models have been employed to describe the population response in V1 in several species.
source: Similar models have been employed to describe the population response in V1 in several species (Goris et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2015; Arandia-Romero et al., 2016; Whiteway et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work using similar models.

claim: The model was cross-validated using a speckled holdout pattern whereby some fraction of neurons were withheld on each trial with probability p=0.25.
source: We cross-validated the model using a speckled holdout pattern (Williams et al., 2018) whereby some fraction of neurons were withheld on each trial with probability p=0.25.
evidence: This is a description of the cross-validation method, with a citation to Williams et al., 2018.

claim: The sign of all latent variables was anchored to the average firing rate of the population, such that positive means increases in the average firing rate.
source: We anchored the sign of all latent variables to the average firing rate of the population, such that positive means increases in the average firing rate.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological choice for interpreting the latent variables.
